tagline.text: A mountain cascade of 20-plus streams spilling down a cliff above the Cagayan de Oro River

location.label: Location
location.text: Tignapoloan (Sitio Impakibel), Cagayan de Oro, on the Talakag, Bukidnon border

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–800 (per person, public transport and lunch; confirm entrance fee and cottage separately)

children.text: Sinulom Falls lies in the mountains northwest of Cagayan de Oro, on the border with Talakag, Bukidnon, where more than 20 streams tumble down a cliff in layers. It is about an hour by car from the city, and the last stretch needs an unpaved road and a walk of about 2 km.

Sinulom Falls sits in mountain country about 45 km southwest of Cagayan de Oro city proper. Sources differ on the administrative location: some describe it as part of Barangay Tignapoloan in Cagayan de Oro, while others place it in San Isidro, Talakag, Bukidnon. The Cagayan de Oro River forms the boundary between the two, and the easiest access is through Sitio Impakibel in Tignapoloan.

The name "Sinulom" is said to come from a Visayan word for black ants. A local story says that during a drought people gathered here like ants in search of water. Residents reportedly came to know the falls around 2002, and as late as 2015–2016 it was not yet an official tourist site, so visitors had to ask permission at a farm guardhouse. Since then the entrance and facilities have been developed, and there are now paid areas and cottages.

Rather than a single drop, the falls is a curtain of 20 to 30 streams running over mossy rock across a cliff face about 100 m wide. The tallest cascade is said to be about 30 m. The water comes from springs and is cold; swimming directly under the falls is restricted, but you can soak in the nearby pools and cold spring. Its biggest advantage is that it can be done as a day trip from Cagayan de Oro. However, the unpaved last section, the roughly 2 km downhill walk and the climb back out demand some fitness and preparation. For visitors who already come for rafting in Cagayan de Oro, it is a good way to add a quiet day in nature.

The part that confuses first-time visitors most is the entrance. Guides mix several routes: the Sitio Impakibel route, the Dansolihon route, and the area with the infinity pool and cold spring. Save the falls' location on your map before you leave, and confirm directions once more with locals at the junction and the basketball court. They are generally friendly and helpful. Allow half a day to a full day from the city for travel, walking and rest. Many reviews suggest about four hours at the site alone, so it is more comfortable to give this falls the whole day than to combine it with other plans.
From a cliff about 100 m wide, 20 to 30 streams drop in tiers. Sources vary between 27 and 30 streams, so confirm the exact count on site. It is so wide that it is hard to fit in a single photo.

blocks.title: A view of the whole falls

children.text: Walking the Sitio Impakibel route, at around
0.5 km
you reach a viewpoint overlooking the whole falls. It is a good place to take in the big picture before the trek.
The water comes from springs and is cold and clear. Even on days when midday highs reach
, a dip of your feet cools you quickly. Some posts say it is safe to drink, but first-time visitors should bring their own drinking water.

blocks.title: Infinity pool and Bolao Cold Spring

children.text: Recent guides mention an infinity-style spring pool and the Bolao Cold Spring area. Since swimming right under the falls is restricted, water play happens in these pool areas. Entry arrangements for each area can change, so follow local instructions.
From where vehicles stop, you walk about
2 km
to the falls. The way down is gentle, but the way back is uphill all the way and takes longer. Along the walk you pass rice fields, forest and mountain village scenery.

blocks.title: The upper Cagayan de Oro River

children.text: The falls feeds the Cagayan de Oro River. In the city it is the river used for rafting, but upstream the mood is entirely different: a quiet valley with few people where you hear the water before you see it.

The path passes farmhouses, fields and small shops. The upland village atmosphere from before the area became a tourist spot remains and is as memorable as the falls. Ask residents for permission before taking their photos.
There are pool areas, and many local families reportedly come with children. However, lifeguards are not always on duty, so keep children close. Weekends get crowded, so weekdays are recommended.

Enjoy the view of the whole falls from the viewpoint first, then head down the slope. If the path is wet, shorten your stride and walk slowly.
Take photos at the falls and pools, eat lunch and rest.
Climb back up and return to Impakibel. One guide says the last jeepney leaves before 15:00, so move early.
Last-transport times can change, so confirm them on site before you go.
Set out from the city on the Cagayan de Oro–Talakag road. It reportedly takes about
30–45 minutes
from uptown near SM City CDO.
About
past Mangalay Bridge you reach the Tignapoloan turnoff. Turn toward Sitio Impakibel.
The unpaved section is steep. In a regular car, park near the basketball court and walk, and check your brakes beforehand.
Rest after lunch and leave in the early afternoon to be back in the city before dark.
You must walk from where you park to the falls, so bring first-aid supplies and water. The climb back is continuous, so leave room in your schedule.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Laguindingan Airport, Cagayan de Oro (CGY), taking about
1 hour 30 minutes

From the airport to the city it takes roughly
1 hour

items.title: Public transport from Cagayan de Oro

children.text: Take a jeepney or van from Carmen Market to the Tignapoloan junction (about
From the junction to Sitio Impakibel, go by motorcycle taxi. The distance is short but the road is rough, so settle the fare first.
Fares and first-departure times differ between guides. Check the latest information on site.
Follow the Cagayan de Oro–Talakag road, pass Mangalay Bridge and turn into Sitio Impakibel at the Tignapoloan junction.
After rain, a 4x4 or spiked tires are recommended.
From where vehicles or motorcycle taxis stop, the falls is about
2 km
away. The way back is uphill, so save your energy.
The dry season from November to May is the best time to visit, with less slippery paths and clearer pool water.

In the rainy season (June–October) the falls is more powerful, but the paths are muddy and slippery. In July and August heavy downpours can make the river rise suddenly, so it is better to avoid those months. Weekday mornings are the quietest.

There is almost no lodging near the falls, and according to one guide overnight stays are not allowed inside the admission area. Most visitors base themselves in Cagayan de Oro and make it a day trip.
There is a small restaurant on site with a few simple dishes and limited choice. Bring snacks, water and a packed lunch, and carry enough cash; there is reportedly no ATM nearby.

Back in the city, we suggest dinner at a restaurant in Cagayan de Oro. It is the main city of northern Mindanao and has plenty of choices. Local eateries are plentiful around the malls in the north of the city and along the riverfront. You will be tired from the trip, so keep the next day's plans light.
Prices for snacks and drinks sold on site may not be fixed, so ask before you buy.
Wear aqua shoes or grippy sandals that stay non-slip when wet.
Bring a waterproof bag, a towel and a change of clothes.
Mobile signal can drop, so download an offline map.
Leaving early keeps you from missing the transport back.
Agree on the habal-habal fare when you board; you can also ask for a round trip.
Entrance fees and rules change often, so check the latest notice.
The spring water is cold, so bring a light layer if you plan to stay in for long.
Bring a plastic bag and carry your trash out. It is remote and bins may be scarce.
Keep ID and small bills handy so paying fees is easy.
Keep your camera and phone in a waterproof case or zip bag so they are safe from spray and sudden rain.
In the rainy season the paths are slippery and the river can rise suddenly, so do not push it after rain or in July and August.
Swimming directly under the falls is not allowed. Stay in the designated pool areas.
Reviews say lifeguards are not always on duty, so always keep children within reach.
Even where there is a diving board, the water is shallow, so do not jump in.
The path is steep and can be hard for people with heart or knee problems.
Some reviews say wooden railings and walkways in places are worn, so take care.

Jeepneys and vans leave when full and the last ones stop early. Be sure to confirm your ride back on site. The mountain road gets dark after sunset, so plan to leave the falls no later than early afternoon.
